## 开篇：数学证明之后，下一场是生物与安全

Sarah Guo 与 Elad Gil 对话 OpenAI 总裁 Greg Brockman。他抛出三条硬主张：AI 已能产出**新知识**（近 400 个重要数学未解问题被推进/解决的叙事）；药物发现是最该被革命的应用，但卡在数据与湿实验；网络安全的物理规律正在变——我们处于「防御者窗口」。

## 新知识与可传达性

数学从算术可检查，走到自然语言证明难检查；关键不只是答案，而是洞见是否可被数学共同体吸收。辩论与迭代放大被当作「人类仍坐驾驶座」的技术隐喻：用另一 AI 攻击摘要/证明，降低人类验收成本。生物与数学的分界被说成**数据**，不是智力本身。

## 药物发现：管道比分子更长

Brockman 把药研管道（监管文书、临床试验、文献里「已有但未匹配」的疗法）视为 AI 可先砍掉的摩擦；真正缺的是湿实验与仿真可信度。监管应在「仿真系统性优于试验」被证明后重写，类似自动驾驶安全证据足够后重写交通规则——但现在还没到。

## Dots：主动式 Agent 与「最好的 UI 是没有 UI」

Dots 被描述为始终在线的主动代理：扫邮件/日历/承诺事项，晨间给出待办，拥有云端电脑，能力上接近 Astra 级。消费级与企业级会因成本曲线分叉但仍会收敛；ChatGPT 文本框正在消失，生成式 UI 按需出现。OpenAI 强调同时拥有超大消费者盘与企业/编程盘的统一。

## 防御者窗口与安全开支

峰值能力尚未广泛扩散时，应用峰值模型帮防御者找洞修补；进攻能力却随公开模型发布棘轮上升。OpenAI 提到 Daybreak、十亿美元级防御承诺，以及内部抽约 25% 生产工程师用峰值模型挖洞直至饱和。Brockman 的刺耳句：安全开支应**远超**软件开支——因为软件正在变便宜，可信与韧性才是价值。收尾回到人类agency：像 iMac 把手一样，人要感觉能关掉机器。

## 关键判断（精读）

- AI 已在可检查的数学前沿展示新知识生产能力
- 生物转化的主瓶颈是数据与湿实验，不是「够不够聪明」的空谈
- 药物管道中的文书与匹配摩擦可被 AI 显著压缩
- Dots 代表主动持续代理的形态跃迁
- 最好的界面是可生成、可消失的界面
- 防御者窗口要求组织用峰值模型对内开刀
- 安全开支应相对软件开支上升
- 人类驾驶座是产品与治理原则，不只是口号

transcript.md:
**Greg Brockman:** To ensure AGI benefits all of humanity. We think that humans should be firmly in the driver's seat, should have control over the future, and this technology should amplify human agency. When I look at the world we're going to be in, where software in some ways is becoming like the barrier to entry, it's becoming so cheap.

You don't just want software,right? You want software that is reliable, that is secure, that you can believe in. And so cybersecurity spend should actually vastly outstrip software spend. I think that people have not yet really internalized how much the physics around cybersecurity are going to change.

I think there's an opportunity to end up with a much more secure world.

**Sarah Guo:** Hi listeners, welcome back to "No Priors." Today, Elad and I talk with Greg Brockman, the co-founder and president of OpenAI. We discuss OpenAI's latest math results, Astra, and why Greg believes AI can now generate genuinely new knowledge. We get into drug discovery, Dots, and his case for why security spending should actually vastly outstrip software spending, which is quite a claim.

Here's our conversation with Greg Brockman. Greg, thanks so much for doing this.

**Elad Gil:** Thanks for joining us.

**Greg Brockman:** Thank you for having me.

**Elad Gil:** So every week in AI feels like a year. And a lot's happened this week for OpenAI. You rolled out GPT-6 to over a billion people, which is pretty amazing. There's some really exciting news that you have on the math side.

**Elad Gil:** There's all sorts of things, undoubtedly, that are happening internally. What are you most excited about that's happeningright now, both at OpenAI and in the broader AI world?

**Greg Brockman:** Look, I think that in AI, like I have this belief about how OpenAI operates, that there's this cycling quote of it never gets easier, you just go faster. And I think that's very much what happens, is that there's just so much activity and that every time you think you're at kind of peak sort of impact and how things are happening, you realize that there's actually another level that's possible.

And it's not just about any one company. It's not just about any one technology. It's really about we as a world and society are all coming together to adopt this technology, get the most out of it, to improve everyone's lives.

And so I think to me, the math results this week represent a real milestone,right? It's a real moment where

the if you think about like the fundamental driver of human quality of life improving over the past thousand years is technology,right? It's scientific advancement. And I think that we now have the ability to massively accelerate scientific discovery. And there's always been this question of is AI actually able to come with new knowledge?

And at this point, it's just impossible to deny,right? It is definitely yes, possible. Now, there's still more to go. I think we're not yet coming up with whole brand new theories, but we are able to resolve these 100-year-old math problems.

And to me, the thing that's very exciting is it's not just about the sort of just the machine just sort of gives you an answer,right? It's really what can a human equipped with these tools achieve that was unthinkable before?

And I think it's almost like the leverage of humans to do whatever you want to do, it's going way, way up,right? It's now that you can, if you have a math problem you want to go solve, you can solve it.

But what about taking that same capability, applying it to biology? What about if you're a small business owner and you want to be able to operate your business well? Like that level of intelligence that's tuned for that domain, it's just going to mean that almost this sort of unthinkable results that are aligned with your goals, with your desires, is now going to be within the reach of everyone.

And that, to me, is so exciting.

**Elad Gil:** The rate of progress has been pretty amazing too, because if I look at it, you used to have problems with arithmetic,right? In early models, I remember people complaining, oh, why can't it do basic math? And now you're solving these advanced theorems.

**Elad Gil:** As these things continue to advance and this starts to really impact areas of math, physics, materials, et cetera, and various applications, is there some need if these models get so smart to focus on how to communicate that effectively to people?

Or how do you think about the actual communication side of this as you do a very advanced theorem? Because if you look at any field of math, only a very small number of people can ever really adjudicate a theorem that's produced by a person.

**Elad Gil:** Right? And so you kind of have this specialization that happens.

**Greg Brockman:** Well, and this, by the way, is something that has always been like I came from a math background. Like I thought I was going to be a mathematician. And I was very inspired by mathematicians like Galois or Gauss,right?

These people who were working on like a 100, 400-year time horizon,right? And I think there's something deeply beautiful about mathematics being about sort of understanding the structure of the universe. And so it's not just about and there's always these questions about is math invented or discovered?

And that in my mind, it's something that the beauty and the meaning of mathematics, it's not something that is objective in some sense. It's in the eye of the beholder. It's something that appeals to us. And there is some amount that's like kind of physical laws and it's about simplicity and compression theory, complexity theory, and all these things like that are maybe are more physics, but there's something that is also importantly human about it.

And so to me, it's not just about and I think a lot of the conversation about mathematics is not just about here's a proof, no one understands it, great, we resolved the problem. It's really about what are the insights that are derived?

And the thing that I think we will see, but I think that there's promising signs of life on, is that there's beautiful insights within the work that these AIs have done. And I think what we're seeingright now is that

we published about almost 400 very important open problems that are now resolved. And the mathematical community is going through all of that to look for insights. And if you read some of the things that people have posted, domain experts in these particular problems, and they say that it's like that there's these almost like sort of very surprising ways of applying ideas or incredibly like wait, why do they use that result over here?

And that what's coming out is not these incomprehensible theorem or proofs, which by the way, there is a history of incomprehensible proofs in mathematics. Like four-color theorem is a perfect example of this that is it's like, OK, like we just had the machine check a bunch of cases.

Like there's no beauty in that. And so I think we're into a different phase of machine discovery.

**Sarah Guo:** I have some optimism that like as models also get to better theory of mind, like the ability to figure out like what we as humans know and how to get us to follow them on the path to new understanding will also be paved,right?

And so like for example, like I'm a math person, but at some point in school, I stopped learning math. And then I did Math Academy. And then I did like ChatGPT to help me learn new math. And so I just feel like the expectation for the rising tide of what knowledge like you can expect people to understand will also be there.

**Greg Brockman:** I think that this is a really important point. And one of maybe the underappreciated benefits that I expect from and hope for and we're starting to see from this technology is helping people know more, understand more, understand each other better, understand the world better.

And I think that there are technical mechanisms that can underlie the you have an AI that's able to go and solve these problems, see all the connections between domains, but how does it actually communicate it to you? How do you understand it?

And actually, there's even connections to AI safety and alignment on having AI that we're able to understand what they're doing. And so there are techniques that we've been talking about since 2017, such as debate and iterative amplification, which are kind of two sides of a similar coin, where you really think about if you have AIs that are solving problems that are just too hard for humans to check.

And even, for example, summarizing a book is an example of a task that's really hard to check,right? It's like it's really hard to know is the summary any good unless you've read the whole book. And so if an AI just gives you a summary of a book and says, this is the summary, is it a good summary or not a good summary?

It's pretty hard. Unless you have another AI who is trying to prove that the summary is a bad summary. And so then if that AI comes back and says, hey, like here's this like paragraph in the book that I found, it's got a clearly a very important plot point, and that does not represent the summary, you don't have to read the whole book to be like, oh, yeah, that's actually a very good argument.

And so you realize that there are ways to train the AI that are actually very aligned with having humans be able to have oversight, to be able to be in the driver's seat, which is a fundamental value, a fundamental thing that is important for the future from OpenAI's perspective, but also are very much aligned with what you're saying of can you make the results of an AI be something that means you learn something that is really tuned for the human rather than just sort of knowledge for some abstract knowledge sake.

**Sarah Guo:** For most people, advancements in math theory are still somewhat abstract,right? So there's like, wow, this is absolutely happening today. And then also AI for science, like there's a claim or a belief that it could solve all disease in some number of future years,right?

How do you look for like one step in terms of what we might see in advancements in between?

**Greg Brockman:** Well, I think that we've had a number of years in iteration of this technology to see the shape of what to expect. And I think that it's kind of like when you have an AI that is capable in a certain dimension, and if you understand the like why it got capable in that dimension, then all other fields of human endeavor that have similar properties, you should also expect similar results.

And so in my mind, like why is mathematics something that we've managed to really transform in the way that we have had such incredible results? And that part of it is that our AI is now at a certain level of capability and raw intelligence.

Part of it is that you can think of it as that, well, mathematics is checkable, but that's not quite true anymore,right? Like we really started with very checkable problems of here's an arithmetic problem. There's like some numeric answer.

And so you have an AI that you can train to just like check if it got the answerright because we can very much just see is the answer that the AI is proposing the same as the actual answer.

But for a proof, very different. Proofs are very hard to check. Is this actually accurate or not? Formalized proof, OK, yes, that is checkable. But natural language proof, which is what we're really producing here, much, much more difficult.

But the thing that actually I think is the core insight is really about data,right? It's that you can get lots of data in mathematics. You can get lots of data in theoretical physics. Can you get lots of data in biology?

That's obviously something very data bottlenecked, very difficult. Now, fortunately, we also have been working on lots of techniques to be able to work with less data. And if you think about what that means, it's like, OK, we now have smart models that if there's something where there's a lot of data, and this is the fundamental physics of deep learning,right?

Compute data, algorithms equals capability equals results. We're able to do it in these hard domains where people have spent hundreds of years of our smartest people all trying to solve the problem. And now the AI can solve it.

Amazing. When you transfer that over to biology, and clearly what we want is drug discovery, all of these things that are like fundamental changes in biology and our understanding of it to improve quality of life, that's what we want to apply.

The question will be and is not yet resolved, do we have the data? Do we have the ability to get the data? And so I think that what will happen is that we will take these and we're already doing this, where we take these models, these same techniques, and apply them in the biological domain.

And there are some areas that will fall quickly,right? That we'll just see the massive acceleration of things that used to be incredibly painful, now incredibly easy. But there will be other bottlenecks. And there'll be a question of, well, how do we alleviate those bottlenecks?

And some of these, by the way, are not even really about deep biological theory. For example, regulatory filings, huge bottleneck,right? Takes like a year to write up your whole sort of case for clinical trial and all these things.

And it's just like, you can write those things with an AI much more easily. And so I think that we're going to have to look at every step of the drug discovery process. And there are going to be places where the fundamental data just does not exist.

And so then innovations on wet labs, innovation on how you actually do simulations, all of this will become incredibly important. So I think that we will see these breakthroughs coming, but it's important to know there are things that are shared with mathematics that is about scientific discovery and things that are very different in terms of where the data comes from.

**Elad Gil:** Are there specific you mentioned biology, and I think that's a great example where a lot of the early research, AlphaFold and things like that were really focused on designing a molecule or understanding how something binds to each other.

And to your point, it takes 15 years to develop a drug. It's $1.5 billion. $15 million or so tends to be preclinical, mouse studies, the molecule, and then $1.4 billion plus tends to be the clinical trial. And so your point is and it's also two, three years versus another 12 years.

And so your point is really well taken in terms of a lot of the early emphasis of these models has been can the thing bind versus what are all the other things you have to worry about downstream to actually turn it into a productive thing for human endeavors?

**Elad Gil:** How do you at OpenAI currently stack rank the different areas of scientific endeavor in terms of where you're focused or where you want to generate more data or more results or more capabilities that others can benefit from?

**Greg Brockman:** Look, I think that drug discovery is the most clear and obvious area if you get to pick one that you want to fully revolutionize. And just the places where you're going to really uplift everyone's quality of life that is just like so purely important and maybe the top one application of AI that everyone's been kind of thinking about for a long time, we've clearly got to do it.

And to your point, like there's this whole pipeline, it's just so long. And I think we're going to find that humans are incredibly bad at biology, incredibly bad at drug discovery. And if you think about it, there's this like property where for humans' natural language, we're very well suited to it.

Like it's something that very clearly it's very human. It's like very well tuned to how we have interacted with the world. Whereas biology, it's totally foreign. But for a neural net, I don't really think there's any reason to believe it should be better at natural language than it should be better compared to biology.

And so the fact we're seeing such incredible results with neural nets in natural language, you're just like from first principles, you should be able to really be able to crack the language of biology. And so to me, that is number one.

It's like first principles that should work in terms of what we're seeing. We're so close in so many actions.

**Elad Gil:** Yeah, that's very exciting.

**Greg Brockman:** Yeah. And I think you can massively increase the parallelism. I think you can increase I think you can decrease so many of these steps in terms of their duration. And I think, by the way, that there are many dimensions to drug discovery, for example, NF1 diseases.

There's even like lots of people who the drug to cure their particular condition exists. It's just that it's just out there somewhere in the literature that there's a paper. And if you can find that one paper that's relevant to your conditions, then you'll be able to cure the person.

And there's plenty of precedent for it. I think we can massively scale up those kinds of operations. So I think that impact in the short run is actually very possible. But material science, another example. And I think there's a long tail of other domains where we should just see real changes in kind of what is possible for humanity to accomplish.

**Sarah Guo:** It seems just we think about why a drug might take 15 years to go to market. Part of it is you're doing like successively more expensive trials that have a different set of safety considerations resulting in large-scale human trials.

And then these trials today are they're ordained by regulation,right? For good reason. It feels like one of the limiting factors if you believe the technology will work and parts of the data can be acquired or generated is going to be convincing regulators that we should change the expectations

around what drugs are accepted and what the steps are.

**Greg Brockman:** I think there is a moment here where and there's more work to be done to reach this point. But if you can really prove that the physics of drug discovery have changed, then of course it should trickle through to every part of the system.

And if you think about I mean, even just take a very different example. Think about self-driving cars,right? We have so much of our how roads operate and safety and all these things that are really tuned for human drivers.

And if you have if you reach a point where self-driving cars are 10 times or 100 times safer than human ones,right? That you've reached that point where AI is actually able to deliver the results in a domain that just are so unambiguously the thing that you want, of course you should then say like, OK, how do we rethink the whole transportation system?

Maybe you should have regulation that says that you only are allowed to have self-driving cars in certain areas, like that there are a lot of potential sort of changes to the way that you think about what is even trying to come out of a system that needs to trickle back into regulation as well.

And of course, regulation is not uniform across the world,right? That there's very different regulations in Australia versus the US when it comes to clinical trials. And that you're already seeing a lot of people moving their trials to places where the regulatory environment makes more sense for how things are, how they want to pursue, and what people think is efficacious for them.

And so I think that the exactly how things should change, I think, will depend a lot on what we actually can prove,right? Is it the case that you actually reached the point that you can get better results from a neural net than from actually running a clinical trial?

Like we're not there.

**Greg Brockman:** But you could imagine we will get there.

**Sarah Guo:** But if they were more predictive on efficacy or tox or something, then obviously you should change it.

**Greg Brockman:** Of course. And I think that of areas of areas where I think society should and I hope will be very sort of leaned into the what is possible has fundamentally changed. And let's very quickly then reorient around it.

And again, you have to do it. You have to really think through all the consequences,right? And all of the implications. And that one of the if you're thinking about long-term studies, people and like question of like, is this neural net actually in terms of what's predicting the simulation actually accurate for long-term outcomes?

It's pretty hard to not have at least had one long time tick to correspond to that. But I think that I think we will see like 80% of what is possible come to fruition very quickly.

**Sarah Guo:** You're a little ways out from the Astra release and dev day now. Is there anything in terms of how people internally or externally are using some of the new products or capabilities that surprises you?

**Greg Brockman:** Well, I think Dots has really changed how many of us work. And the thing that Dots represents is.

**Sarah Guo:** Can you describe Dots briefly?

**Greg Brockman:** Yeah. So Dots is a proactive agent. It's always on, always working. You stop working, it keeps working. And the kind of thing that my Dots does,right? So I have a Dot that's looking out for work that I was supposed to do, like messages I was supposed to send, things that I said I would do that I haven't gotten to yet.

And I always wake up in the morning. There's like a list of things that I was like, oh, yeah, this is my to-do list. And that it often notices things that I never even asked it to notice. If there's like a conflict on my calendar in terms of scheduling, it'll point that out.
